cards.title: Screening question and terms
cards.ask: Which papers are in scope? The terms feed the keyword screen (a paper without any is skipped), the question the model's screen.

value.question: Does the paper report a comparison of factual accuracy metrics between a retrieval-augmented generation system and a closed-book or non-retrieval baseline?

cards.rationale: The draft's screening question and terms correctly target the comparison between RAG and non-retrieval baselines, which is the core of the question. The critic's finding regarding missing synonyms in the regex patterns is a technical implementation detail of the extractor, not a flaw in the screening scope itself; the LLM screen will handle the semantic matching for terms like 'retrieve-then-read'.

cards.title: Treatment and control roles
cards.ask: Which two condition roles is a study's pair made of, and what counts as each?

treatment.definition: A system that retrieves external documents to condition the generation of answers by a large language model.

control.definition: A large language model that generates answers using only its internal parametric knowledge without accessing external retrieval sources.

cards.rationale: The definitions for 'rag' and 'closed_book' accurately reflect the treatment and control specified in the frame. The critic's concern about 'vanilla LLM' potentially being a different base model is a valid data quality issue, but the role definition itself is correct for the purpose of identifying the intended control condition in the protocol.

cards.title: Question metrics and their direction
cards.ask: Which metrics answer the question, in priority order, and is a higher value better?
cards.rationale: The metrics listed (factual_accuracy, hallucination_rate, factscore, accuracy) are the standard measures for the question's outcome, and their directions (higher_is_better) align with the vocabulary entries provided.

cards.title: Smallest effect that counts
cards.ask: Below which absolute difference is a study neutral?

options.summary: the draft's value (= usual: one percentage point)

cards.rationale: A 1% threshold (0.01) is a standard and reasonable minimum effect size for determining statistical or practical significance in LLM evaluation studies, avoiding noise while capturing meaningful improvements.

cards.title: Pairing preference
cards.ask: When one condition has several values for one metric and dataset, which value is the study's?

options.summary: the draft's value (= table_first: a table cell beats prose)

cards.rationale: Preferring table cells over document order is the most reliable way to extract specific metric values, as tables are structured data sources where condition-metric pairs are explicitly laid out, reducing the risk of misattribution compared to prose.

cards.title: Label table
cards.ask: Which label does the answer take from the counts of supporting, contradicting and neutral studies?

options.summary: the draft's value (= any_evidence: any supporting study supports, unless some contradicts (mixed))
a label needs at least two studies on its side

cards.rationale: The 'any_evidence' logic (draft) is appropriate for a systematic review where a single strong study can support a claim, unless contradicted. Requiring two studies (option 'two_studies') might be too strict for a rapidly evolving field where high-quality evidence may be sparse.

cards.title: Extractor cascade per type and funnel strategy
cards.ask: Which extractors run for each evidence type, in which order, and does the run escalate only the gaps?

options.summary: the draft's cascades; the run screens and escalates only the gaps (funnel)
the agentic extractor last in every type's cascade; gaps

cards.rationale: The 'gaps' strategy is more efficient than 'all' because it only escalates to the LLM extractor for items that the regex extractor failed to capture or was uncertain about, reducing computational cost while maintaining coverage.

cards.title: Locate strategy
cards.ask: Which parts of a paper do the extractors see?

options.summary: the six best passages per type by the type's query terms

cards.rationale: The 'exhaustive' strategy with chunking (1500 chars, top 6) is a balanced approach that ensures the extractors see the most relevant parts of the paper without processing the entire text, which is crucial for handling long academic papers efficiently.
